chapters.html:
Before the Evernight blanketed the lands, and the foul Tide began its campaign, the city-state of Kios was once a bustling trading hub, welcoming hundreds of travelers each day through its open gates. A great temple to the fair Talanton stood proud in the city's center, around which a bountiful market flourished; balance coins oft traded hands, and at all hours of the day, the shouts of vendors peddling their myriad wares and shouts of haggling could be heard.

Diomede once minded the noise, all those years ago. She'd peer out the doors of her clinic, brow furrowed in anger, at those noisy merchants. A garden lay between the clinic and the market, and yet, the sound carried through the vine-draped trellises and flowering shrubs. What an annoyance, she thought, to have to listen to that din at all hours.

But Titans, dear Titans above, does she miss it now.

She still waits in the clinic, in the quiet remnants of the once-busy town, waiting for travelers. They don't come by much anymore, but enough do for her to stay.

Most of her time is spent reading at the clinic's front desk. A young man used to be her attendant, as she was far too busy to triage patients herself. He begged her to come along with everyone else who fled when the Tide first came, said that Kios's Council promised safety in the great city of Okhema and that if she stayed here, she'd surely die. Of course, she refused to follow.

Who else will tend to the injured if not her? So long as travelers continue to limp through her doors, broken and bleeding, she's needed here. If the Tide consumes her, so be it. Her sacrifice will not have been in vain.

Today, whenever that day might be on the calendar that she can no longer track in this perpetual twilight, she hears the slow, steady footsteps of an approaching dromas outside. She closes her book, but doesn't rise from the desk; she's placed signs outside the clinic and has the lights on to signal that she's here, so if these travelers need her, they can come to her.

A minute later, and the door is pushed open. A lone man enters. A heavy crimson cloak obscures his form, but from what she can see, he appears to be in good health. His blond, shoulder-length hair is kempt, some of it knotted in a neat braid that hangs by his neck. His features are sharp but not gaunt with hunger. His eyes are clear, unclouded by pain.

"Hello, do you require a doctor?" she asks, the words rasping in a throat rough with disuse.

"Not for the time being, no," the man replies. His voice is deep, and though he doesn't speak loudly, there is something about him that demands attention. "I'm on an expedition with a group of my soldiers, and we were planning to stop here for a day to rest. Is it acceptable if we set up camp near your clinic?"

"I don't own this city, you're free to do as you please."

"If you're the only soul left, doesn't that make it yours, in some sense?"

She sees something in those eyes when they meet hers, something powerful and terrified in equal parts. The sharpness of a warrior meets with royal self-assurance, and then beyond that is fear, well-concealed but not invisible, not to those who spend their lives reading others.

Who is this man? She will not ask, but she will wonder.

"Perhaps. But I don't claim ownership--truly, if you're concerned, then don't be. It's acceptable if you camp nearby, and if you need my assistance, I'm happy to offer it."

"If you're certain. Thank you for your generosity."

She's left alone for a quint, listening to the faint sounds of conversation as this man and his soldiers pitch their tents and settle down for their rest. A few come in, asking for medicine for minor ailments and bandages for small wounds.

The armor they wear is unfamiliar to her, as she's not the worldly sort, and she can only guess what city-state they may be from. They seem to be competent warriors, considering how few injuries they've sustained despite the ever-present danger of the Tide surrounding the city. Perhaps they're from Okhema and are on some sort of mission; she's heard recent travelers speak of some Chrysos Heirs, and the soldiers' leader seems authoritative enough to be a person of great import.

Again, she will not ask. Whatever happens beyond the crumbling walls of Kios is not her problem, not anymore. All she'll do is treat these soldiers and send them on their way.

Eventually, she presumes she's tended to all of them, as she's left alone once more. The sounds outside have quieted--they must've gone to rest. She takes inventory of her supplies, and then returns to her seat at the counter to read until sleep decides to come for her as well.

But then, just as her eyelids begin to droop, the man re-enters, this time approaching her instead of lingering at the entrance. The metal plating of his armor clatters with each soft footfall. He's gentler than she would've guessed. It makes her like him more; she's never appreciated the travelers who stomp around as if they own this place.

"You're more than a field medic," he notes, without greeting, after surveying the certificates on her walls.

She blinks back the sleep in her eyes before responding. "I am a doctor, yes. I received my training at the Grove. Just know that I lack many supplies out here, and there are surgeries I cannot perform."

"Can you test for pregnancy?"

The question, asked cautiously, gives her a moment's pause. She hasn't been asked for such a test since before Kios was abandoned--the travelers that come by here aren't ever in such a delicate condition.

"I believe I can, but allow me to check my storage."

On a bottom shelf, covered in a layer of dust, she finds the vial she seeks. A thin, clear liquid is inside, made from hollyhock sap and Aquila's purified tears. It still seems acceptable for the test despite its age; even if it weren't, she can't hope to make any more of it with her meager supplies, so it will have to do. She brings it back to the man, along with a sewing needle sterilized with pilfered whiskey.

"Lance a finger with this, and squeeze a drop of blood into the vial. Swirl it around for a minute, then let it sit for another. If the liquid turns green, it's positive."

The man accepts the items with a polite nod, and immediately turns to leave.

"Wait a moment," she says, before he can make it out the door. "Inform whomever this is for that they may come to me for assistance should the test be positive. I can provide some supplements or a termination, whichever is desired."

She's not certain, but based on the way the man's posture stiffens, she thinks it may not be for anybody but him. Despite her suspicions, she won't press. If he really is with child, he's free to decide his next move.

"... I will."

The man does not return to her.

She drifts off at her desk for a dreamless, dark sleep, and when she awakens, a peek outside reveals that the group has departed. They didn't stay for long, they must truly be on an important mission , she thinks.

It shouldn't matter to her, and yet, she finds that her feet have carried her to the remnants of the camp, prying eyes scanning the ground. Nothing has been left out in the open; they cleaned up well after themselves. So, she looks elsewhere. There's a small planter at the edge of the plaza, full of long-dead plants, that she bends down to inspect.

Just as she anticipated, she finds it there: the vial, discarded in secret.

The liquid contents are a bright, undeniable green.

After a journey of three months, one would think that the sight of the Holy City imminent on the horizon, promising long-awaited respite, would bring joy to the weary caravan of soldiers.

But the mood is somber. Their journey, and all their struggle along with it, was in vain.

As Mydei sits atop the back of his dromas, he's not sure what to focus on. The weight of failure sits heavy and uncomfortably within him, but ignoring it brings another issue to the forefront of his mind, which is currently manifesting itself as a persistent nausea. The swaying stride of his dromas does not make the latter any better.

He swallows thickly, and decides he'd rather consider his failure.

There will be much to brief Aglaea on when they reach Okhema's gates in the next quint, and he must be prepared. She had high expectations of them, of him especially. He is, after all, the Kremnoan prince. If anyone in this world could locate the lost Castrum Kremnos, it would be him.

So far, three months of constant searching offered nothing. Not a single hint, not the smallest of traces, no, nothing but dead ends. It's almost as if his birthplace has vanished off the face of the earth--which it hasn't, certainly not, but the level of elusiveness is not encouraging.

Okhema's Council is already at odds with the Chrysos Heirs, and if they continue this stalemate of inaction for any longer, Aglaea's command over the city will begin to slip. She's promised much to the people, all promises insofar undelivered. At this point, having failed to find any of the remaining Coreflames, their inaction has become glaring.

"Young lord, what troubles you?"

It appears Krateros has finally decided to break the silence that has settled between them. Mydei hasn't been up to conversation for weeks at this point, and he knows he's been short with his master. Frankly, he expected to be reprimanded for his behavior much sooner.

But Krateros doesn't seem particularly upset, now that Mydei's looking at him. He seems almost worried--a rare expression to see on his face. For all of his master's strengths, he's never been the emotional type. He cared for Mydei in his own unique manner, which involved a lot of intensive training and gifts of weapons.

"I believe it is obvious what troubles me. We failed in our mission."

He thinks it's a suitable enough explanation on its own. Krateros is also upset, he must understand. The only reason he agreed to help lead an expedition sponsored by Lady Aglaea in the first place was for the promise of finding his homeland. Mydei being the other leader also helped, but in the end, his master has always longed for one thing: Castrum Kremnos.

"There is more to it than that, isn't there? You've been out of sorts since before we reached Kios."

Mydei tries, and fails, to come up with some explanation. He isn't out of sorts, he's been completely normal, he wants to insist--but that would be a blatant lie. Krateros is right, despite Mydei's best efforts to conceal what's been happening to him. There is so much to hide, so much to accept, so much pain to prepare himself to feel. And while everything else is still safely concealed within his mind and under his traveling cloak, his dour mood has been impossible to shake.

"... It's nothing that should concern you."

Being dismissive rarely works, but perhaps Krateros will accept it.

"Any trouble of yours is mine as well. Your mother charged me with caring for you, and I shall, even when you refuse my assistance," he replies, tone a bit sharper.

So he won't accept it, Mydei muses, unable to stop a scowl from twisting his features.

"It's not something you can help with, master."

"Nonsense. I'll decide if it's really beyond my reach, but you must inform me first."

Mydei opens his mouth to bite back a reply, but then closes it, contemplating. Now is not the time to tell him; however, he must find some way to get the matter dropped before then. If there's one person in the world more stubborn than himself, it's Krateros, so this will be a difficult task.

He gets two seconds to think before the dromas takes an uneven step due to a rock, and the jostling movement is enough to make Mydei's stomach lurch. His hand flies up to cover his mouth in a desperate attempt to hide his violent, full-bodied gag. Based on the look Krateros gives him, he fails.

"Young lord?"

Mydei wills the nausea away as he takes a deep, shuddering inhale through his nose. For a moment, it seems to abate, but then, his stomach lurches again, more insistent. Shit, he's going to be sick. There's no way for him to escape, to do this out of sight like he has been for the past two months.

"Young lord, what's wrong?"

His response is grabbing the nearest receptacle, which happens to be an empty bag of rations, and retching up bile until his throat burns.

How long does it take before the taste of his own acid-tainted saliva stops making him gag? It feels like hours. Krateros is there, saying things to him, rubbing the space between his shoulders, but Mydei can't focus on anything but his misery. By the end, he's breathless, gasping for air as if he's been drowned.

"... That is what's wrong, master," he finally says, before tossing the ruined bag a distance away behind their caravan. "I'm ill."

"But you do not get ill."

"I do, on rare occasions, but they are not typical illnesses. I'll have to go to the Twilight Courtyard. As I said, there is nothing you can do about it--you are not a follower of Aquila."

It's not an outright lie, but is a lie by omission, he supposes. At least Krateros accepts it this time.

"I see why you chose not to inform me. You'd hate to admit weakness and hand more responsibility to me--but I wouldn't have minded, you know. It is not a weakness to be afflicted by an illness, it is simply an inevitable occurrence in life. Do heed my lesson, young lord."

"Yes, master," he mumbles, before falling silent once more. He doesn't have the energy to talk any longer, and thankfully, Krateros doesn't insist on furthering the conversation.

The last quint of their journey is entirely uneventful. He rests his eyes for a while, knowing he'll need the energy for what is to come.

When they finally pass through Okhema's gates, Mydei feels no relief, as his teleslate instantly buzzes. Of course, it's a notification from Aglaea, telling him to come to the Mamoreal Palace as soon so he can debrief her on the results of the expedition.

She must be able to sense his dejection through her threads already, but she wants to hear it from him in person for the formality. Lovely. He informs Krateros that he's needed urgently before leaping from the dromas's back in a fluid, easy move. It's off to the palace for him.

He expects to find Aglaea in the reserved baths, but riding the lift up shows them to be entirely empty, save for Castorice, who appears to have dozed off. She startles to wakefulness when he approaches, her hand moving to clear the curtain of hair that fell before her eyes.

"Lord Mydei, you've returned. It's nice to see you again."

"Likewise, Lady Castorice. Lady Aglaea says she wishes to meet with me for a debrief, have you seen her?"

"Ah... I believe she's in the meeting room with a few Council members who also wish to hear the summary of your expedition."

He swears under his breath. "The Council is involving themselves?"

"Unfortunately."

With renewed haste, he makes his way to the meeting room. To say this is not good would be an understatement. There are a few ways this could be worse--it could be Elder Caenis herself requesting a meeting, or it could be taking place at the Dawncoud--but the outlook is grim enough as-is.

When he steps into the meeting room, he represses his natural urge to scowl as the Council members turn their gazes to him, as snide and disdainful as ever. He doesn't recognize the three of them, which means they're not important officials. It's easy to draw a conclusion: Elder Caenis isn't too engaged in the results of the expedition, and she likely only cares because Aglaea sponsored it, not the reason for it in particular.

In all honesty, he despises these political games. Perhaps that is not the opinion a future king should have, but knowing his duty and wishing to carry it out are two very different things, and his wishes do not align with endless arguments concealed as orderly debates.

Stiffly, he bows, and takes his seat at the head of the table. The world doesn't care much for his opinions--he's here, ready to play this game once more. He'll even mind Okheman manners today. Will his efforts go unappreciated? By the Council members, certainly, but Aglaea might thank him later, and he does assign some value to her opinion.

"Welcome back, Lord Mydeimos. What news do you bring from your expedition?" Aglaea asks, breaking the icy silence with her ever-impassive words.

He takes a deep breath before launching into his explanation. He details their entire expedition, including every place they went and curio they encountered. They went to abandoned city-states with previous ties to Kremnos, stumbled across artifacts and fragmented texts from long before the Black Tide claimed his birthplace, even found a lone Kremnoan soldier who escaped without joining the detachment, instead choosing to wander the Evernight.

But in the end, despite everything, it all boils down to a short sentence: we found nothing.

"... I see, that's unfortunate," Aglaea says mildly, once he's finished speaking.

One of the Council members, an older man, huffs. "Would you not describe this expedition as being an unnecessary use of supplies during a period of conflict? That would go against Okheman law."

"We couldn't have known it would be unsuccessful before it was conducted. The Chrysos Heirs have many abilities, but foresight is not among them."

As always, Aglaea is an expert at handling the Council, and the man can only huff once more before quieting.

"If you have no questions regarding the contents of the expedition itself, then I shall dismiss Lord Mydeimos and allow him to recuperate after his difficult journey."

When no protests are made, Mydei graciously accepts Aglaea's offer. She must be able to sense his exhaustion through her threads, or perhaps his appearance is evident enough. He manages another bow to the Council members before egressing.

It takes the last of his remaining energy to march through the palace with his posture intact; the instant he's reached his chambers, he slumps, all tension leaving his body in an instant. Titans, he can't remember being so tired in all his life. There was much he did not include in his explanation of his trip--none of it was pertinent for them to know. His own personal issues were more taxing than any single experience.

When did the trouble first begin, but the morning--or what they knew by their pocket watches would be morning were they not basked in constant darkness--he awoke to find the familiar haze of pre-heat had not yet settled upon him as he had anticipated.

He was never thrilled to welcome his cycle until he reached Okhema a few years back and was finally given the miracle of suppressants to completely quell any of his body's natural urges. So, while his estrus cycle happened to line up with the expedition, a few days shy of being a month into it, all he had to do was take a week's course of suppressants at his cycle's advent to soothe the beast.

If only that advent arrived. Perhaps it was stress, he reasoned, as the constant exertion and somewhat slim rations they had been afforded could certainly mess with his hormone levels, though his estrus had always been like clockwork in the past, even during his days in the detachment, when stress was a near-unbearable constant at all hours. Poor sleep, lack of nutrition, the threat of Eurypon's fury crashing upon them at any moment, terrible grief, and the imbalance of his adolescent hormones had not disturbed that clockwork.

Strange, yes, but no reason for disconcert, not yet. Then an entire two weeks had gone by, there was still no trace of pre-heat, and it dawned on him, as insidious and forceful as a riptide, that mere stress was not the reason. A new reason for its absence was presented to him, one that was not as easy to swallow.

The next day, the nausea began, and afterwards, there was no more denial, only a resigned hunt for confirmation that he found in the derelict city of Kios.

As he's mused on his misfortunes, his body has already gone through the motions of disrobing--pointedly done with his eyes trained upwards, not looking down at what is becoming of his physique. Now, he slides into bed, eyes squeezed shut with determination, mind forcing all of those unpleasant thoughts out to allow him to rest peacefully.

Tomorrow, he'll face it. For now, he craves nothing but the darkness behind his eyelids.

It was another brutal action hour in the Month of Everday, which is to say that Phainon is utterly miserable. He forwent wearing his cloak in the morning, but it hasn't done him much good. Sweat has entirely soaked his back, and he is infinitely glad that Aglaea decided his undershirt would be black when she designed this outfit; already red-faced and panting, he doesn't wish to imagine how much worse he'd look trudging through Okhema if the sweat-stains were visible.

Now that it's parting hour, Phainon can finally take a break. And how desperately he needs that break with the weight of his exhaustion now bearing down upon him.

The baths are only a short distance away, he reminds himself, as he walks up the sloping path to the Mamoreal Palace. He's already made it to here from the training grounds, he can manage another few minutes.

He doesn't register who else is in the Heroes' baths, only strips down and lowers himself into the coolest one with an abject sigh of relief. Dear Titans, this is exactly what he needed.

The reason for his exhaustion is, as usual, the exercises he just completed. Without Mydei around to spar, he's been forced to do boring, repetitive sets that do nothing to improve his swordplay, only make muscles he didn't realize he had ache terribly.

Would he get overheated sparring with Mydei? Of course, but at least he would be having fun, and getting riled up enough would inevitably lead to a later tangle in the sheets. That made it worth it--to have a purpose for his suffering.

Mydei will be returning tomorrow, or so Aglaea promised, way back when he was first sent off on that long expedition. Phainon penciled the date onto his calendar and has checked it religiously each day in anticipation of his return, as devout as any worshiper.

"Snowy!"

Phainon's broken out of his reprieve when Tribbie and Trianne flutter over to him from Aglaea's side--he didn't notice she was here either, though he's not particularly surprised--Trinnon close behind.

"Decided to enjoy the baths at this late hour? You must've had a long day," Phainon greets with as much vigor as he can muster.

"Honestly, we weren't too busy today. We wanted to speak with Agy for a bit, but afterwards, Trianne wanted to play, so we stayed for a while longer."

"And it was a good idea!" Trianne crows.

"Excellent to hear. It certainly sounds better than what I've been doing," he mutters. "Oh, how bored I've been..."

Tribbie cocks her head. "You're bored? We thought you'd be spending time with De."

"He's not yet returned, how could we spend time together?"

"He returned a day ahead of schedule," Aglaea provides, "I met with him last quint to discuss his journey before sending him off to rest."

Phainon barely manages to grab a towel to preserve his dignity in front of the Tribios as he shoots upright. He's never felt as motivated as he does at this moment, drying himself so quickly his skin feels raw and then forcing himself back into his sweat-soaked clothing.

He'll finish his bath later. Right now, he has a much greater priority.

He just barely remembers to call out a goodbye as he hurries away, and he catches the high-pitched giggles of the Tribios in response, along with Aglaea saying something he can't quite make out, but sounds like her scolding him for his impatience.

How can he be impatient when he's been so patient already? It's been ages since Phainon walked the path to Mydei's chambers--three months, actually, but ages to him. The path is as familiar as ever, and then there it is, the door to his chambers, unremarkable at first glance due to its similarity to all the other doors in the hallway, but significant because it's Mydei's. Phainon knocks thrice, perhaps a bit too forcefully from his excitement, and announces himself.

Yes, he has the spare key, and can let himself in at his leisure, but barging in while Mydei is still recuperating would not be very considerate. So, he waits patiently to be granted permission, long enough to wonder if he may be asleep. An impatient itch goads Phainon to knock once more, though he resists the urge.

And after a pause, his patience is rewarded.

"Come in."

Phainon unlocks and pushes open the door, a beaming smile easily settling on his face as he takes in Mydei's scent. Oh, how he missed it. It's sharp, spiced in a manner reminiscent of myristica, and ineffable in its nature, much like the man himself. Above all, though, it reminds Phainon of home.

He allows himself to bask in it for another moment, to take another inhale-- and then the confusion arises, because there's something different.

What about Mydei's scent has changed? Phainon's never had the keenest nose, and he can't tell exactly what it is, all he knows is the presence of something new has inserted itself into the notes, something deeper and richer, almost recognizable, but just out of reach.

He approaches the bedside, hoping that perhaps scenting him directly will provide some more clarity, but looking at Mydei shows that he is not so open to the affections he would normally accept without explicit permission. His neck, and scent glands by extension, are covered by the thin sheets he's drawn all the way up underneath his chin. He lays on his side, back to the door, face presumably staring at the other, mostly barren wall.

This is not how Mydei rests. He may have been asleep earlier, considering how the night-curtains are drawn, but he hasn't been for a while. There's an alertness in his body, an almost unbearable tension strung up in the air around him, that would suggest he's on guard.

"What's the matter?" he asks carefully, maintaining some distance between the bed.

"... Our mission was unsuccessful. We couldn't locate any trace of Castrum Kremnos."

Phainon sits on the edge of the mattress, taking his willingness to answer as an invitation. "It's eluded everyone, don't be too hard on yourself. If we all keep working at it, we'll stumble onto it eventually, I'm certain."

He reaches out to pat Mydei's covered shoulder as a gentle reassurance, but he flinches so violently the moment Phainon's fingertips brush against it that he immediately draws his hand away while his vocal chords, without his input, produce a terribly pathetic whine. He can't help himself--this is too strange, and some alpha part of him reacted on its own instinct-driven accord.

Are they mates? No, but that never mattered in the past. Mydei would prefer to call them lovers--that's probably the best word for it. They're not bonded by anything formal or biological, but Phainon still thinks of him as his mate. Lovers, after all, feels too vague to him, and much too fancy. He called him his boyfriend once, which made Mydei wrinkle his nose in distaste and remark that the term is too juvenile. So, mate will do.

And to some deep-rooted, instinct driven part of his brain, this is as real as a mate's rejection. The sinking feeling in his gut, the tightness in his chest, the chill prickling across his skin--it's an amalgam of shock and embarrassment that has him debating if he should rip open the night-curtains so he can fling himself out of the window. He has to make this right, he can't bear to watch Mydei suffer.

"There's more to it than that, isn't there? Did something bad happen? Please, you know you can tell me anything," he tries again, but to no avail.

"Nothing bad happened besides the obvious," Mydei insists. "I failed, and that is all. It's unimportant."

"But it clearly is important."

"Stop asking."

There's a dangerous edge to his tone that makes Phainon's skin crawl. Pushing further seems like a bad idea.

Mydei's here in front of him after so many months, and yet he's still untouchable. It's too much, Phainon needs to make him crack, needs that vulnerable part of Mydei to bear itself to him.

"Mydei, please--"

"Just leave me alone!"

Phainon only begins to process the words shouted at him until his feet have carried him out of the room. They ring in his ears and slam around the inside of his skull, as confounding as they are painful. He finds himself sitting on the nearest bench, head cradled in his shaking hands, eyes burning with tears threatening to fall.

He doesn't understand. After so many weeks apart, he thought their reunion would be joyous. He expected Mydei to smile with one of his hard-earned grins, to welcome him into bed alongside him to rest together once more. He didn't ever expect to be kicked out like an unwanted stray--because why would he?

Mydei's never acted like that before, never, not even when they first met. And over the years, Phainon's become a close confidant. When Mydei's troubled, he'll tell him without hesitation. They trust each other. They're comrades in arms and lovers in private. In body and mind, secrets come undone, revealed by lips and hands.

If Mydei won't tell him what's wrong, then it can mean only one thing.

Mydei doesn't trust him anymore.

And that revelation hurts worse than death itself.

The rest of the quint passes with him in a daze, wandering around Okhema like a spirit on its way to the Netherworld. He doesn't know what to do with himself anymore. The tightness in his chest does not fade, and he can't breathe properly, no matter how hard he tries to force it. He feels as if some crucial part of his machinery was ripped out; without it, he's a husk of himself.

Somehow, he makes it to a tavern. Other patrons are starting to file in as action hour comes to an end, but there's still an open seat at the bar. He collapses onto it and orders to his heart's content.

Phainon doesn't drink, not in any regular frequency. He'll have a glass of wine when the situation calls for it, but beyond that, he has no interest in the intoxication of alcohol. It dulls his senses and makes him vulnerable in more ways than one.

But right now, he needs it. Each shot of whiskey and cup of mead soften the edges of reality, distancing himself from the pain of his mistakes in the most efficient manner.

He still doesn't understand what those mistakes may be, but it's certainly his fault. Why else would Mydei reject him so plainly?

Godsdamnit, he doesn't want to think about Mydei, but now it's all he can think about. He's started crying, a thoughtless stream of tears staining his cheeks and landing upon the bar, joining the droplets of condensation from his half-empty water cup. The bartender gave it to him, said something about being worried about him, but he hasn't finished it.

Drinking was a terrible idea, why did he think it would make this better? It's only made his mind too sluggish to work through the battering waves of emotion, allowing them to overwhelm him entirely. Perhaps he hasn't gone far enough--if he drinks himself into unconsciousness, then it won't be his problem anymore, not until the morn. He raises his hand to flag down the bartender, when--

"By Zagreus's balls, what the hell is wrong with you?"

Suddenly, the seat next to Phainon is occupied by perhaps the last person he wants to see right now: Cipher.

Is the universe just toying with him?

"Leave me 'lone, I don't... ugh... need your mockery," he moans, weakly attempting to push her away but completely missing. His palm slaps against the bar counter and Cipher, unimpressed, stares back at him.

"I'm not gonna mock you when you're like this. Kick a man when he's down and all that. Did your boytoy break up with you or something, why do you look like a lost widower?"

"He's--he's not my 'boytoy'... don't call 'im that."

She gives an exaggerated eye roll, but relents. "Fine. Did your boyfriend break up with you?"

"Maybe? I dunno... dunno what happened. He came back from his expedition today, and-and he... He just wouldn't talk to me, he... pushed me away, I don't... Didn't even..."

"You're not making sense right now, Titans above. Your liver's barely hanging on. Hey bartender, get me a cuppa Georios's tonic, and make it quick!"

"No, nono... I don't want-t that," he slurs, but is powerless to stop as Cipher forces his mouth open and pours the foul liquid down his throat. The awful taste does bring him back to himself, coughing and spluttering as it carves a searing path down his throat.

He's not sure what sort of remedy the Grove formulated to dispel intoxication so quickly, but they need either an award or to be punched.

"There we go, now start from the beginning, tell me what's up."

Venting to Cipher seems like the worst idea possible--who knows what sort of ammunition that would give her--but since she's been so attentive, he decides to tell her a very brief summary. It's not as if there's much to say in the first place.

"Hmm... Yeah, that's a puzzler," is Cipher's intelligent reply. He resists the urge to smack her.

"Is that all you've got? Seriously?"

"Woah, why's Okhema's Deliverer yelling at me? I didn't do shit, I'm just a pretty kitty giving some advice--"

"You didn't give any advice! You just shrugged!"

"Okay, maybe I didn't, but you gotta cut me some slack. Whatever you and Mydei have going on is weird."

"You're one to talk, you and Aglaea always--"

"That's not the topic of the conversation!" she sing-songs. "C'mon, tell me more about your boytoy. What's he like, what sorts of valuables does he have, how much gold is in that necklace he wears--that kinda stuff."

He sighs heavily and pinches the bridge of his nose. If there's one thing Cipher's good at, it's making one so annoyed that they forget all their other troubles.

"I'm not telling you that... Just give me some sort of helpful advice, please?"

He already knows he's erred by begging her. The shit-eating grin she gives him is indication enough that he'll never live this down.

"I dunno, I wouldn't place all the blame on yourself, I don't think you made a mistake. He was cagey the moment he returned, yeah? So, you couldn't've done anything."

"But what could have happened on such a perilous expedition? He spent all of his time fighting and investigating, as far as I'm aware."

"Maybe he cheated on you and feels guilty? Look man, I gotta head out, you can puzzle over this yourself."

Cipher's gone in a quantum flash, leaving nothing but a coupon on the bar stool for some sort of event--there's a picture of a shirtless man with oil dripping off his chest, which is enough to prompt him to rip the thing in half. What use did she think he'd get out of that? It's certainly not a consolation after what she said.

She's lucky she left so quickly; if she lingered after suggesting that Mydei, of all people, cheated on him, he would've actually throttled her. Mydei would never. Such an egregious breach of trust goes against his very essence.

So, it's impossible. Whatever is going on must be more complicated, and if Phainon just tries talking to him again, after he's had more time to rest, it'll go better. There's no need to blow this out of proportion.

Tomorrow, Phainon resolves, he'll get this all worked out.

Finding Mydei is an escapade that takes almost the entirety of lucid hour, as he doesn't respond to any of Phainon's messages, and isn't in any of his usual haunts. After walking halfway across Okhema, asking random Kremnoans if they've seen their prince, examining the training grounds top to bottom, and even pleading with Aglaea to use her threads--which she refuses to do--he finally stumbles across him looking at one of the artifacts in Theodoros's shop.

Phainon is in such awful shape at that point that he debates just turning around and trying again when he isn't sleep-deprived and sweat-soaked. But after all that effort, he can't bear to give up right when he's managed to succeed, so he works up the courage and marches over, willing himself to act more composed than he feels.

"Mydei!"

He whips around upon hearing his name, instantly on edge. It hurts Phainon to see, but he forges ahead, closing the distance between them until they're mere paces away. Mydei doesn't seem to be in better shape than himself, with sleeplessness haunting his eyes and an almost sickly pallor. He's not dressed in his armor, instead draped in a loose chiton that doesn't appear to fit him. Again, Phainon wonders what's actually the matter, but shelves his curiosity.

"... Deliverer," he greets stiffly, "why are you here? Aren't you busy?"

"Aglaea didn't give me any assignments, so I thought to patrol Okhema for a while. I'm glad to have run into you! I wanted, uh... I wanted to apologize for how I acted yesterday."

"You wanted to apologize? For what do you have to apologize?"

"Well, you'd just returned from a grueling journey, and I barged in asking you all those questions. I should've waited until you were feeling better, but I was impatient. So, I'm sorry."

"You were simply showing concern, as you are wont to do. Though I feel it's unnecessary, I'll accept your apology, and we'll put this matter behind us."

If Phainon didn't know Mydei as well, he'd be content. The matter's resolved, and all should be well--but something's still wrong. Deeply wrong.

"Is it alright if I ask what happened during the expedition to upset you?"

The shift in Mydei's already tense demeanor is instantaneous. Any vulnerability is gone. His jaw clenches and he breaks away from Phainon's gaze, eyes darting around as if searching for an escape route.

"... It wasn't anything important, just an issue with my master. It will be resolved soon enough. Frankly, it's none of your business. It doesn't involve you."

Mydei's never been a good liar--he never bothers with it. So, Phainon knows every word of his excuse is nothing but a poorly-constructed attempt at deception. But he doesn't comment on it. There's no need, not when they're both aware.

What matters to Phainon is the delivery.

Though he's speaking quietly, he's using the same forceful tone as yesterday--and now that Phainon can see his expression, it's obvious that it's not anger, but fear driving his response.

Mydei is afraid of him.

And perhaps Phainon stares at him in silence for a moment too long, because Mydei jolts, taking a large step back as one of his hands flies up to grasp almost desperately at the side of his neck.

"What?"

"Nothing, I just..." he trails off, at a complete loss. His words, the most useful tool in his arsenal, fail him, and he's left to scramble for footing when the floor's been pulled out beneath him.

How could Mydei be afraid of him? Mydei isn't afraid of anything, not war or blood or death--or anything. But Phainon knows how to read people better than he knows himself. He knows what fear looks like.

And it doesn't make any sense.

"... Why are you scared?"

The question slips out before he can bite his tongue, because as much as he wants to bury this mess so he doesn't have to deal with the discomfort of trying, letting it fester will only make it worse, and the consequences would certainly destroy him.

He needs Mydei, doesn't know what his life would be reduced to if Mydei wasn't in it. If he had to beg for forgiveness at his feet, prostrate himself in front of the entire city, bear the slings and arrows of scorn for even a chance, then he'd do it in a heartbeat.

But he doesn't get a chance. Mydei takes another step back, and Phainon knows it's all slipping through his grasp. It's more than the physical distance--it's the chasm yawning between their hearts.

"You're being ridiculous, I'm not scared. Perhaps you should go to the Twilight Courtyard to check if you have any screws loose. And I myself have business elsewhere, so I'll be off."

Even when Mydei has long since vanished from his sight, Phainon stands frozen in place, eyes trained at the horizon, a part of him hoping that maybe he'll come back, will admit to all his troubles so that Phainon can put it all back together, will let him give him the kindness he's missed for the last three months.

Gods, he still doesn't understand--understands even less than yesterday. The only certainty is that he keeps making things worse with each word he says.

Maybe this is all he's ever been good at, ruining things. He's haunted by something unknowable, some specter that rips and tears and bleeds people dry, that burns villages to ash and ash to dust, that brings life to wither into ruin, and even the person he thought would weather the storm of himself is drifting away.

And he can't bear the thought. He needs it to go away--if it lingers any longer, it may just burst from his skull into reality. He has to run from it, hide where it can't reach him, and then he won't lose him, everything will be okay and it has to be because he can't take the pain anymore and-- He finds himself sitting on a secluded bench in a public garden when his mind manages to process his surroundings again. He doesn't remember a second of his walk here, though it's a nice spot to have a crisis; a fountain bubbles away happily to his left and the leaf cover blocks out the worst of Kephale's light.

Breathing is difficult. Seeing is difficult. But he forces himself to exist again, piece by piece, until the world doesn't feel like it's closing in on him.

It's progress, though not much. His legs feel like lead and any attempt at standing would likely fail. How long will he be stuck here until his body starts functioning again? Perhaps the rest of the day, perhaps an eon--

"Mama?"

Something, someone, is tugging on his pant leg. He glances down to find a young girl, no older than four, looking up at him expectantly. She's dressed in the Kremnoan style: simple and functional, with robes cut at the knee to not impede running. Her auburn hair is neatly braided in the back, with a golden hair clip keeping some fly-aways from drifting in front of her dark brown eyes. The hand not gripping his pants is clutching a plush lamb to her chest. "Oh. You're not my mama," she says quietly, before he can respond.

No matter how terrible Phainon might feel, he's not going to ignore a child who's obviously gotten lost. He takes a deep, painful inhale, blinks his stray tears back, and gives the girl a bright smile.

"I don't think I am, young miss. Do I look like your mama?" he asks, mouth feeling like he's been chewing chalk.

She gives him a thorough appraisal before shaking her head. "No... But your shoes are the same color."

"Ah, I see how that might've been confusing. But fret not, I'll help you find your mama."

With a new mission to tackle, he bullies his legs to cooperate and gets up with a huff. He offers a hand to the girl, not really expecting her to take it, but to his surprise, she's quick to latch on.

"Alright, where should we start... Were you in these gardens with your mama, or somewhere else? Do you remember when you last saw her?"

"I was in the garden wit' mama... She was sitting on the bench like you 'cause her feet hurt real bad, and I was sitting wit' her, but then I saw a purple butterfly and... umm... I chased it even d'oe she told me not to run away from her... She's gonna be mad..."

"I think she'll just be happy to see you! Maybe she'll scold you, but only because she's worried, not because she's mad."

That seems to placate the girl, and she doesn't voice any more concerns as they make their way through the garden in the direction she came from. It's not a particularly large garden by any means, though it must feel like a vast forest to her. He makes sure to walk slowly, letting her take in the surroundings at her leisure.

It's more peaceful than any other time he's returned a lost child, considering how often refugee caravans approaching the city get attacked and separated. Though a harrowing mission is rewarding in its own right, he appreciates the downtime. He's not in the right headspace for anything more intense than a brisk walk.

When the girl eventually slips her hand from his grasp, he nearly has a heart attack, but turning in her direction reveals that she's running towards a woman sitting on a bench, one who bears a striking resemblance to her. She's wearing similar clothing, though altered to accommodate for her obvious pregnancy, and all her features match up; additionally, the relieved smile on her face when she catches sight of the girl acts as confirmation enough.

"Iris, there you are! I was about to call mommy to help look for you," she says, while reaching out to ruffle her hair. "And look at who you stumbled across on your adventure. Greetings, Lord Phainon. I can only assume you found her?"

"She found me, honestly, but yes, I supported her on the last leg of her adventure."

She huffs out a laugh. "Of course. I hope it wasn't too much trouble for you. I'd have gone looking myself, but... Well, you can see the state I'm in. I believed I could handle a short trip to the gardens, but I've overestimated my current abilities again. My life as a warrior is behind me, yet I can't seem to shake it."

"I'm always happy to help, don't fret! And for a member of the Kremnoan detachment, doubly so. Whatever goodwill I can extend to your people is well worth my while, Lady...?"

"Otonia. Let us drop the honorifics, just call me Otonia. After all, you're good friends with our prince, aren't you? That makes us comrades."

Phainon valiantly ignores the pang in his heart as he responds; if ever there was a time, it isn't now. "Good friends, rivals... Both are apt descriptors. He's a very honorable man in every sense."

"... Prince Mydei gives me candies sometimes," the girl--Iris must be her name--adds quietly, "and he found Sheepie when I dropped her in the market. He's nice."

Dear Titans, if this keeps up, Phainon's heart is going to give out, though from sadness or longing or affection, he's not sure. All three, probably. He's not sure how he's able to love one person so ferociously.

"Indeed he is. I've always worried about the Kremnoan children, even before I had my own, but as long as I've been a part of the detachment, I've seen him keep watch over them. Compared to old Eurypon..." Otonia waves her hand dismissively. "Well, I don't think they're comparable at all, that's the sort of difference between those two. But that's enough about our prince--you must already know this yourself. I'll let you get back to your duties."

"Though I'd love to chat, I should be getting back to the Mamoreal Palace, you're right. I'm honored to have helped you, Otonia. Farewell, I do hope we meet again!"

He musters up his most convincing smile for the pair--the moment he's turned around, it cracks.

Godsdamnit.

Everything hurts and he's so, so tired. These last few days have been an endless gauntlet of torment that he's not meant to endure. He can't keep running--the memory of Mydei is inescapable.

What is he supposed to do with himself now?

He just barely manages to return to the bench, knees buckling the moment it's underneath him. His body slumps. A wheezing breath sighs from his lungs. A shaking hand rises to catch his head.

He's such a mess. He can't even think straight anymore; Otonia’s words loop insistently, echoing, drilling into his psyche. They only made small-talk, it shouldn't be so significant, but a strange sort of heaviness blankets his mind, like a fractured memory is trying, yet failing, to claw to the surface.

He can't shake the feeling that he's missing something.

Two weeks.

Two long weeks have passed since he returned, and Mydei isn't sure if he can take another minute of it.

The latest target of his frustrations--an already-brutalized training dummy-- is punched so hard that its head goes flying across the training grounds. A guard practicing footwork has to duck out of its way. Mydei would typically offer some apology for interfering with another person's training, but the thought of trying to talk is currently unbearable.

He's mad. About what, exactly, he's not sure. It's probably hormonal, but he's not going to go to the library to read up on his current condition. He's already experienced his condition enough for the day considering he spent a quint hunched over in his washroom vomiting.

The next dummy explodes when he uppercuts it, its straw innards spilling onto the sand. He gives it another punch for good measure, and hardened shards of blood spike from the site of impact, shredding what remains of its body into tattered ribbons.

It's somewhat satisfying, though it fails to scratch that itch in his mind that begs for a real opponent. He'd like to find a sparring partner, but he's not in control of himself. Losing himself in battle is too easy when he's in a bad mood. Battle is how he calms himself, as once his body is exhausted, his mind lets go of the day's troubles, though the more troubles have piled up, the more intensely he must fight to banish them.

Who could manage to keep up with his myriad frustrations today? Phainon. No matter what Mydei throws at him, he'll always raise his blade to parry, and then riposte. Training isn't going to get him anywhere, he finally decides. He's not sure what to do instead, but if he stays here any longer, he'll destroy all of the training dummies, and there won't be anything left to entertain him. So, after drying his face of sweat, he sets off to wander the city.

It's rare that he has such an abundance of free time to waste on an aimless walk. It does calm him down, he supposes, to spectate Okhema's beauty. Of all the places he could've settled down, this is probably the nicest; the citizens may not be fond of him and his people, but the cityscape is easy on the eyes with such verdant greenery, the food is palatable, and the training grounds are above satisfactory. Mydei's simple wants are easily met.

But no matter how breathtaking the city may be, it's boring to stroll around by oneself. He can only stare at flowerbeds for so long before he becomes restless from inaction. His only current desire is to fight something, fight someone, and he knows that isn't going to happen.

The main issue is that Aglaea still isn't sending him out on missions. She must assume he wants a few more weeks to readjust to his normal life after such a grueling expedition, but he, at least, doesn't think it was particularly grueling. He's endured much worse, after all.

It just won't work, he knows he can't have Phainon and the child both, but he wants to believe that there's some way to manage it, that some perfect solution will fall right into his lap if he just stalls for time.

Life is unfair. This was his very first lesson, taught to him through the burn of salt water in his infant lungs, the wordless begging for his mother with pure, instinctive feeling in a mind that had never learned any language beyond terror, the weak strikes at shapeless beasts that would drag him under each time he fought to surface--how could he ever forget?

But his wanting for a family of his own shouldn't be beyond reach. It's a simple wish, so simple that when he first expressed it to Krateros many years ago, his master scoffed, and said that he'd certainly have it once he reclaimed his crown. It almost goes without saying.

So, why must it be impossible? He doesn't wish to dwell on Phainon's rejection, which still stings as fresh as it did when he first heard it, though at this point, he can't banish it from his mind, not when the man himself is meters away, sulking, acting like this isn't his fault as well.

Gods, he feels sick.

"Lord Mydei, could you tell us again what you saw in Tretos? A great core of--"

"I must excuse myself, Professor Anaxagoras."

It's a miracle he makes it to the washroom sink before he vomits. There's not much to lose, he hasn't eaten all day, but his body insists on choking up the water in his stomach.

This, by far, is the worst symptom of pregnancy. Nothing brings him such abject misery as watching himself steadily wither away as each day without proper nourishment passes by.

And it only gets worse when somebody enters the washroom while he's still hovering over the sink, gripping the basin so tightly he's left gouges in the stone with his gauntlets. He must fetch the Tribios to rewind it or find some way to pay for the repairs; however, he must field some questions first.

"I'm sorry for following, but the others insisted I check on you," Hyacine says gently, once he's stopped retching. "Are you alright, Lord Mydei?"

He debates what to say while he rinses his mouth out. An answer of 'nothing' would be quite foolish, considering who's asking him. Hyacine is a doctor, a brilliant doctor at that. He's not surprised she was sent to help.

If he's being honest with himself, she might just be the best person to tell. She'll probably be able to help with these troublesome symptoms, and he knows anything he tells her will not pass through her lips, no matter who asks.

Now that he's being offered the opportunity on a silver platter, he supposes he should take it.

"... How long is 'morning sickness' supposed to last?"

It only takes her a second to piece things together. Momentary shock ghosts across her features, quickly overtaken by her usual composure.

"In what sense?"

"I'm in the second trimester, which is when it is meant to abate. It has not."

She hums in thought. "Well... It varies by person, though if you've used suppressants for an extended period of time, it can be worse. The nausea is caused by elevated hormone levels typical in early pregnancy, but an imbalance can result if hormone level has been low for many months. I would guess this is such a case."

He's not pleased to hear that, but it's an explanation. He sighs, then draws back from the sink. For now, at least, his stomach has settled.

"Is there any way to suppress the nausea?"

"Certainly! I normally wouldn't be able to prepare a prescription for you so quickly, but considering the severity of your morning sickness... It troubles me. Excuse me for my bluntness, but you look rather gaunt. I can only guess you've not been eating properly for many weeks now."

"You're correct--but don't trouble yourself for my sake. I can endure for longer."

It's more of a lie than he'd care to admit, but the promise of a cure should tide him over for at least a few days. Hyacine doesn't accept it regardless.

"It's a simple medicine to make, it's really not any trouble, especially when you're suffering so greatly. I know how much you value your physical health. By the end of the day, I'll have it ready for you, and I'll personally drop by your chambers to deliver it!"

"Thank you, Lady Hyacine," he says quietly, "and do let the others in the meeting know I won't be returning. I need to lie down for a while."

"I will. Rest well, Lord Mydei."

Feeling the confrontation has concluded, he makes for the door, but she clears her throat as he brushes past her, stopping him.

Her voice is scarcely a whisper, words a secret meant for his ears alone. "If you want any other assistance from me, just send me a message. Certain procedures are outlawed in this city, but that will not stop me from caring for my patients. The Council should not have control over your body."

"... I will keep your offer in mind."

He does consider it--he's been considering such an option since he first suspected his pregnancy. Unlike the close-minded elders of Okhema, his own people have never seen the termination of pregnancy as something taboo. If he, their crown prince, were to deny them the continuation of their legacy, he knows they would not care. If Mydei were to have told Krateros back on their expedition, even he, with all his expectations, would've made him an abortifacient himself.

But that's not the outcome he wants.

As Mydei retreats to his chambers, he cannot stop a hand from resting upon the swell of his abdomen.

The circumstances may be far from ideal, but he will not be deterred. This is his child, and he will protect them as long as he is able. He will birth them, raise them, and guide them in a kinder world, one much gentler than the horror he's known.

His only regret is that he must do this without his mate by his side. He always imagined himself celebrating each moment of pregnancy with another, sharing in the joy a child brings. To bear life is a great honor, and the ability is a strength like no other. Such an undertaking is not to be done alone, or with uncertainty--it should be done freely, with purpose, and above all, with happiness.

Oh, how he wants to be happy.

What a pathetic wish that is, one of a sad child more than a warrior. But a part of him has never grown up, left eternally as a fledgling life thrashing within a sea of death. He can't fault that boy for his wants--he deserves far more than what he got.

It's a shame that Mydei can't grant wishes. No matter how hard he fights, there are many things that are out of his reach.

What a sorry state of affairs.

The moment he's laid upon his bed, he curls on his side, once again allowing his imagination to wander, to dream that Phainon is beside him, draped over him in that endearing way he does, like he wishes to fuse their bodies together. His face would be buried in the scent glands on his neck, arms wrapped around him to cradle him and the child both, legs thoughtlessly intertwined, skin pressed against skin.

He plans to allow himself but a moment of weakness, and yet now that he's at rest, the memory prods at his conscience once more, demanding his attention. More than a year has passed, and yet, it is as clear as glass, preserved in full despite how little he wishes to remember.

And without his nausea to distract him, he has no choice but to recollect.

Up until action hour, it had been a perfectly fine day, pleasant but not notable by any means. He'd had a simple breakfast, trained with Phainon, soaked in the baths, then gone out for a stroll in the market. They'd just finished up a difficult mission a few days prior, which meant Aglaea had granted them a rather indulgent week of rest. Mydei, of course, was already getting bored with no assignments, so Phainon had been spending his days dragging him around to entertain them both. That particular day, he wished to look at a pottery stall with some alleged quality goods.

Mydei knew nothing of artifact appraisal, and he had no way to verify if they were authentic. Phainon seemed to think they were, but after staring at the same amphora for twenty minutes, he'd given up, and said he wanted to ask his mentor for advice. So, they'd gone to Theodoros's shop, only to find it closed for the day.

"Huh... He's on a trip to the Grove, I forgot he told me that last week... whoops. Guess I'll just have to buy the amphora and hope it's real."

Mydei had scoffed. "This is why you never have any funds, you're always so quick to spend them, on suspect goods no less. Curb your impulse and hold off on the purchase."

"And this is why your chambers are so barren--you never buy any decorations," Phainon shot back.

"They're not not barren, they're organized. Your chambers are so cluttered I need a map to navigate them."

"It's not that bad and you know it. They're charming. Cute. Pleasing to the eye. A work of art, even."

"Lady Aglaea would have a conniption if she saw what you--"

Before their argument could progress any further, Phainon was nearly bowled over when somebody ran into him. It was a young Kremnoan boy-- Mydei instantly recognized him by his distinctive red hair.

"Crap--oh my gods, Prince Mydei, Lord Phainon! I'm so sorry!" the boy, Sostias, had said, instantly falling into a bow. He was ten at the time, and rather short for his age, but very determined to become a warrior regardless.

His fathers were both accomplished fighters in the detachment and former members of the Godshield brigade, so his ambitions weren't surprising.

"There's no need for such formality," Mydei had insisted. "Regardless, do be more careful where you're going, and don't roughhouse in the market. You could fell a weaker warrior with a single blow if you don't mind your own strength."

"Yes, Pri--... uh, Mydei! I'll be super careful next time, I promise. Hey, Cory, get over here, he's not mad!"

From the shadows, Sostias's friend slunk out, looking a bit frightened. "I'm very sorry..."

"Do not cower, young Corydon. Both of you have great strength, there is no shame in that--but there is a time and place to show it. The best warriors know when to sheath their blades. Now, if you wish to spar with each other, do it at the training grounds in the Kremnoan district. If they refuse you entry due to your age, tell them Mydeimos said you may enter. Just remember to be careful, stay away from other trainees, and use the wooden practice weapons."

The boys both nodded enthusiastically, and then scurried off, presumably to the training grounds. Phainon had chuckled, though he didn't say anything on the matter until they'd begun walking back toward the Mamoreal Palace.

"You really like kids, don't you? You always make time to talk with them, and you're actually nice, too."

"I have responsibility over the Kremnoan children, of course I'm attentive. I would be a horrid prince if I wasn't. I must greet each new arrival, grant them Kremnoan citizenship, ensure they're raised to be honorable members of society with all the necessary resources at their disposal--these are my duties. Though we may never return to Castrum Kremnos, our culture will be preserved, I will ensure it."

"That's noble of you... But it doesn't answer my question. I mean, you'll play with the Okheman children too."

"I do on occasion, only because I'm roped into their games."

"Really?" Phainon pressed, one eyebrow quirked, clearly not believing his denial.

Mydei had finally acquiesced--there wasn't much point in pretending anyway. "I am rather fond of children, I suppose you're correct. Raising them properly is an undertaking that is duly rewarded. I've always wanted some of my own, I'd like to have that experience myself."

It was an easy admission for Mydei to make--not insignificant, but not unnatural, either.

"... Some of your own? With... with me?"

"Of course. You are my equal, and the only mate I will take. I've always envisioned this as our future--"

"But it isn't," Phainon suddenly interjected, almost breathless. Mydei glanced over to him and felt something in him lurch.

The face he was making was familiar but so unwelcome. A dreadful sort of fear had seized him, obvious in the hang of his jaw, the paleness of his skin, his blown-out pupils--and the glaze in his eyes, like he was looking a thousand miles away, not at the man right in front of him.

He only looked this frightful when he was having an episode, when the grief of his past became too great to ignore and dissociated him from his body and mind, to the extent that he wouldn't even recognize the other Chrysos Heirs. He'd lie in his bed, chest heaving, whimpers of terror slipping past clenched teeth, body caught in some intangible battle.

It had been years since he'd last suffered one, but Mydei's innocuous comment had brought him back there in an instant.

And for once, he was at a loss for words, for action, for anything. All he could do was watch.

"You can't have--... Not with me, please no, you..." Phainon managed to gasp, before fleeing, actually fleeing from Mydei's side.

Where Phainon went afterwards was not something Mydei tried to uncover. He instead returned to his own chambers and spent the rest of the day reading over the latest Council decree regarding the detachment, noting down sections that he'd have to negotiate with them later. He'd been putting off the task considering how little he enjoys political dealings, but not wanting to be idle with his thoughts spurred him into doing it.

Phainon did not just run from things. When faced with armies of Titankin or Tide-twisted abominations, civilians with horrific injuries he hadn't the skill to mend, Council members shouting at him with all the venom they could muster--Phainon would step up and do what needed to be done. The word 'retreat' did not seem to be in his dictionary, even if it was ill-advised.

But Mydei had scared him off. Scared off the man he'd quietly hoped would always stand by his side, who wouldn't be taken from him like all the others. The last thing he'd wanted to do was think about the damage he'd done to his most cherished partner.

Had he actually ruined their relationship?

To his utmost surprise, Phainon arrived at his door while he was still working, smile looking only a bit awkward, with a peace offering in the form of a fresh plate of golden honeycakes.

"Hi... Sorry about that," was all he said. He'd obviously been crying, but Mydei didn't comment on that, only sighed and let him inside. He was too relieved to see him return, nothing else mattered.

"I'll clear off my table, we'll share the meal."

Phainon's smile brightened at his words. He tentatively launched into a story about something that had happened at the diner as he was getting the food while Mydei packed up the scrolls littering his dining table that was seldom used for dining.

The meal was awkward at first. Mydei prepared himself for a confrontation, and yet, he just couldn't find the words, not when Phainon seemed so eager to put it behind them.

So, they did not speak of the matter again.

Mydei knows he should've followed him that day, should've asked what, exactly, the problem was, should've done anything but pretend as if it never happened while it ate him up inside. But with his rejection of the idea so plain, Mydei decided there was, indeed, nothing left to say.

It's quite clear: Phainon doesn't want children with him.

At the time, he was alright with the prospect. Children didn't, and still don't, have much of a place in their lives, so rife with danger and packed with work. Mydei had long since tucked the dream away in the lockbox of his mind, knowing that it would have to wait until the Era Nova was upon them.

With such odds stacked against the chance of conception, it's a miracle that it happened now--a miracle in his mind, anyway. Phainon might not think the same.

Mydei believes in the strength of Phainon's character, but in this matter, he's not proven himself. He'd much rather flee than confront even the possibility, and offered no chance of discussion regarding it. An unnecessary retreat is a shameful thing to any warrior worth their salt.

Or is it?

Quite suddenly, he thinks he has a viable plan.
